# Batting Averages

::: {layout-ncol="2"}
![](images/derek-jeter.jpg){fig-alt="Derek Jeter baseball card"}

![](images/david-justice.webp){fig-alt="David Justice baseball card"}
:::

## Batting Averages

Consider the following data:

| Batter        | Year | Hits | At Bats | Average  |
|---------------|------|------|---------|----------|
| Derek Jeter   | 1995 | 12   | 48      | .250     |
| David Justice | 1995 | 104  | 411     | **.253** |
| Derek Jeter   | 1996 | 183  | 582     | .314     |
| David Justice | 1996 | 45   | 140     | **.321** |

## Batting Averages
To summarize, David Justice is a better batter....

::: fragment

| Batter | Hits | At Bats | Average |
| ------ | ---- | ------- | ------- |
| Derek Jeter | 12 + 183 = 195 | 48 + 582 = 630 | 195/630 = **.310** |
| David Justice | 104 + 45 = 149 | 411 + 140 = 551 | 149/551 = .270 |

:::

[Wait, what?]{.fragment .emph .cerulean-dk .large}


## Batting Averages

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)

ba <- tibble(player = c("Jeter", "Justice", "Jeter", "Justice"), year = c(1995, 1995, 1996, 1996), hits = c(12, 104, 183, 45), at_bats = c(48, 411, 582, 140)) |>
  mutate(ba = hits/at_bats)
ba_sum <- ba |> group_by(player) |> summarize(ba = sum(hits)/sum(at_bats))

ggplot(ba, aes(x = year, y = ba, color = factor(player))) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") + 
  geom_hline(data = ba_sum, aes(yintercept = ba, color = factor(player)), inherit.aes = F) + 
  geom_text(data = ba_sum, aes(x = -Inf, y = ba, label = paste(player, "Overall\nBatting Average")), inherit.aes = F, vjust = 0.5, hjust = -0.1) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1995:1996) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Jeter" = "#0F2439", "Justice" = "#B21028")) +
  guides(size = guide_legend("At bats", override.aes = list(linetype = NA, fill = NA)), color = guide_legend("Player", override.aes=list(shape = NA, fill = NA))) + 
  theme(legend.background = element_blank(), legend.key = element_rect(fill = "white"), legend.box = element_blank(),  rect=element_rect(fill="white")) + 
  ylab("Batting Average")
```

## Batting Averages

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)

ba <- tibble(player = c("Jeter", "Justice", "Jeter", "Justice"), year = c(1995, 1995, 1996, 1996), hits = c(12, 104, 183, 45), at_bats = c(48, 411, 582, 140)) |>
  mutate(ba = hits/at_bats)
ba_sum <- ba |> group_by(player) |> summarize(ba = sum(hits)/sum(at_bats))

ggplot(ba, aes(x = year, y = ba, color = factor(player), size = at_bats)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") + 
  geom_hline(data = ba_sum, aes(yintercept = ba, color = factor(player)), inherit.aes = F) + 
  geom_text(data = ba_sum, aes(x = -Inf, y = ba, label = paste(player, "Overall\nBatting Average")), inherit.aes = F, vjust = 0.5, hjust = -0.1) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1995:1996) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Jeter" = "#0F2439", "Justice" = "#B21028")) +
  scale_size_area() + 
  guides(size = guide_legend("At bats", override.aes = list(linetype = NA, fill = NA)), color = guide_legend("Player", override.aes=list(shape = NA, fill = NA))) + 
  theme(legend.background = element_blank(), legend.key = element_rect(fill = "white"), legend.box = element_blank(),  rect=element_rect(fill="white")) + 
  ylab("Batting Average")
```

[Times At Bat is a **lurking variable** that explains why the overall batting average is unexpectedly different from the by-year batting average]{.emph .sage-dk}

# Simpson's Paradox

## Simpson's Paradox

::: {.callout-note .large}
#### Definition: Simpson's Paradox

A phenomenon in which a trend appears in several groups of data but disappears or reverses when groups are combined

:::

Arises from 

- confounding variables
- clustered data
- failure to manage causal data
- extremely different rates or amounts of data across categories


## Simpson's Paradox, Visually

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-alt: 
#|   - A scatterplot with 300 observations showing a negative relationship between x, which lies between 0.8088 and 15.6080, and y, which lies between -5.2918 and 9.0437. As x increases, the value of y decreases. A linear trend line highlights this relationship. 
#|   - A scatterplot with 300 observations showing the relationship between x, which lies between 0.8088 and 15.6080, and y, which lies between -5.2918 and 9.0437. There are six groups of points, and within each group, there is a positive relationship between x and y, however, the group means show a negative relationship between x and y. A set of six linear trend lines, one for each group, highlights this relationship. 
#|   - A scatterplot with 300 observations showing the relationship between x, which lies between 0.8088 and 15.6080, and y, which lies between -5.2918 and 9.0437. There are six groups of points, and within each group, there is a positive relationship between x and y, however, the group means show a negative relationship between x and y. Both the overall and the within-group trend lines are shown, highlighting the different ways we can interpret the relationship between x and y. 
#| fig-cap: 
#|   - Negative association between x and y
#|   - Positive association between x and y, within each group
#|   - ???
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-extra: fragment
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(2093467)
n <- 300 
p <- 2  
x <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), nrow = n, ncol = p)
# Define Sigma, the target correlation matrix
sigma <- matrix(c(
  1.0, 0.5,
  0.5, 1.0
), nrow = p, byrow = TRUE)

# Cholesky decomposition
L <- t(chol(sigma))
diag <- diag(c(1,1))
y <- t(diag %*% L %*% t(x))


df <- tibble(group = rep(1:6, each = 50),
             x_mean = rep(c(1:6)*2+1, each = 50),
             x = x_mean + y[,1],
             y = 10-x_mean+y[,2])

ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = F, color = "black")

ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y, color = factor(group))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = F) + 
  scale_color_manual("Group", values = c("#f16278", "#f58220","#124734", "#6b9e85", "#01add8", "#288dc2"))  

ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y, color = factor(group))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = F) +
  geom_smooth(aes(x = x, y = y), color = "black", method = "lm", se = F, inherit.aes = F) + 
  scale_color_discrete("Group")
```

::: {.incremental}

- When interpreting results, it's critical to explain both the group-wise trend and the overall trend.    
[This can get complicated]{.fragment .emph}

- Data ethics means explaining things in **context** and not stopping at the first plot or model    
[Even if the first plot or model matches your expectations]{.fragment .emph}

:::

# Lies, Damned Lies, and Statistics

## Ethics

::: incremental

- Understand how the data was collected
  - potential biases
  - missing observations
  
- Understand relationships between variables
  - including variables that may not be present in the data

- Interpret results with humility
  - allow for the possibility that you don't have all the information
  - consider how data, model, or interpretation might be wrong
  
- As a consumer, be skeptical, especially when results confirm your prior beliefs

:::
